extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians/philosophers of mathematics, and readers interested in mathematical methodology (particularly algebraic geometers and those studying rigor and objectivity)
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing rigor and objectivity in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical-historical analysis of different notions of mathematical rigor and objectivity, focused on the Italian school of algebraic geometry and on how types of rigor (small-scale/formal vs large-scale/substantial) impact reliability, shareability, and the practice of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor as formalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor is associated with the possibility of formalization: a proof is rigorous if it can be converted into a formal proof (i.e., with enough time, energy, background knowledge and logical skill, one can produce a formal proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalizability is taken as the received view in philosophy of mathematics; formalization is continuous with usual mathematical procedures (Avigad). This view implies that being correct means one can supply details to any level of precision, down to axioms and rules of a formal foundation. Example: formal proofs/checking with proof assistants (Coq, Lean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-scale rigor (formal rigor / local rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small-scale rigor concerns decomposing mathematical inferences into smaller inferences and eventually basic inferences; it enables local, step-by-step grasping and mechanical checkability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-scale rigor underwrites intersubjectivity and shareability: a simil-proof has small-scale rigor iff it enables local grasping. It is necessary for systematic checking and for eliminating unnoticed mistakes. Anti-patterns: arguments lacking small-scale rigor cause communication impasses; but excessive microscopic detail can also obscure overall strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large-scale rigor (substantial rigor / holistic rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale rigor pertains to the macroscopic, organic structure of arguments and theories — awareness of overall strategy, relations among major lemmas and known results — and is linked to faithfulness to mathematical facts and to intuition/visual 'seeing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale (or substantial) rigor can guide discovery and provide a form of justification via holistic grasping (as with Enriques, Castelnuovo, Severi). It may rely on geometric intuition and thought-experiments. Anti-patterns: when not connected to small-scale rigor, it can be unshareable and allow errors to persist; it can be elitist (accessible only to extraordinarily talented 'visionary' practitioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local grasping
rubrics_metrics.description: A local, step-by-step grasping of how (if at all) the argument supports its conclusion, plus acceptance of its premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local grasping is what small-scale rigor enables; it is the practical ability to recognize each step as a valid logical consequence of earlier items. Important for mechanical checking and for rendering arguments intersubjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic grasping
rubrics_metrics.description: A holistic grasping of how (if at all) the argument supports its conclusion, involving awareness of the large-scale structure of the argument, overall strategy, and how it relates to known mathematical areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic grasping is what large-scale rigor enables. It can make arguments more compelling to experts and facilitate discovery, but may be obscured by excessive fussy detail. Good presentations balance hints of overall strategy with sufficient detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simil-proofs and their reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Simil-proofs: arguments that look like proofs to relevant agents and are accepted as proofs after checking, broadly satisfying community standards of acceptability; they may nonetheless contain fatal errors. Reliability is the degree to which a simil-proof is likely to be a genuine proof (correct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigor (in its senses) underwrites the reliability of simil-proofs. Comparing reliability of simil-proofs (not of proofs) is meaningful: more reliable simil-proofs are more likely correct. Simil-proofs vary in type and may embody different kinds of rigor, enabling different forms of grasping (local vs holistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability of mathematical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is shareable if its content and supposed correctness could be grasped by relevantly trained human minds from a (possibly enthymematic) perceptible presentation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability is required for arguments to function as agreed-upon evidence and for objectivity as intersubjectivity. Non-shareable forms of justification (e.g., purely private 'seeing') fail this test. Ensuring shareability typically requires small-scale rigor or at least presentations that make the structure graspable to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as faithfulness to the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity conceived as the aim of correctly describing facts — if a claim is objective, it correctly describes some aspect of mathematical reality (the 'facts out there').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception aligns with practitioners who think of mathematical objects quasi-concretely; large-scale rigor and mathematical 'seeing' can better track mathematical facts for some practitioners. Limitation: this form can be elitist and insufficiently shareable if not recast into small-scale rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as intersubjectivity (absence of personal bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity conceived as freedom from personal biases: scientific/mathematical results are objective to the extent that personal biases are absent or are removed by social processes; results are intersubjectively agreed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieved via shareable arguments and small-scale rigor that allow trained peers to check and agree. Democratic and essential for a mathematical practice to flourish and be communicable. Contrast with faithfulness-to-facts notion which can be elitist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor's functional role: enabling grasping
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor functions to allow relevant audiences to grasp how an argument supports its conclusion; rigor is conceptualized as what underwrites the possibility of such grasping (local or holistic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties rigor directly to reliability of arguments: small-scale rigor supports local grasping; large-scale rigor supports holistic grasping. Both are valuable and often coexist; problems arise when one exists without adequate connection to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between detail and overall strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mathematical presentation balances sufficient local detail (to allow checking and local grasping) with enough indication of overall strategy (to allow holistic grasping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: excessive 'fussy' deductive detail that obscures the overall strategy can reduce reliability for human readers; conversely, leaving too few details or excessive reliance on intuition/vision can prevent local grasping and checking, leading to communication impasses and unnoticed errors (historical example: parts of the Italian School).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization/intuitive 'seeing' as justificatory practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical 'seeing' — quasi-perceptual visualization or intuition — can serve as a form of justification for some mathematicians, giving a direct confidence in propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable only insofar as these visualizations can be recast into arguments that others can grasp; otherwise they are non-shareable and threaten intersubjective objectivity. Examples: Enriques's 'seeing' and the 'little dog' anecdote; some areas (low-dimensional topology, classical Italian geometry) heavily rely on visualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal mechanization and machine-checkability
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proofs (or mechanized proofs via proof assistants) present proofs 'pixel-by-pixel' enabling machine readability and mechanical checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They ensure small-scale rigor and maximal local grasping (even by machines or those who 'cannot see'), but may lack helpful hints about overall strategy and thus hinder holistic grasping for human readers. Use case: interactive proof assistants like Coq or Lean; printers/pixels analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical practice viability criterion: shareability and communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: For a mathematical practice/methodology to flourish it must be shareable and communicable; methods carried out only by exceptionally talented individuals cannot sustain a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices should aim to integrate faithfulness-to-facts (discovery) with intersubjective shareability (checking and teaching). Historical lesson: the Italian School produced important results but lacked shareability in places, leading to errors and fragility of the practice until modern methods reconciled the approaches.
